headline: Southwest Ledge Goes Quiet at Noon, Comes Alive After Dark — Bonito Window Cracking Open
subhead: Bass have pushed deep into the structure through the heat of the day, and the first temperature break that could carry albies or bonito is finally showing on the meter.
body_markdown:
I felt it before I saw it Tuesday morning — that flat, oily calm off the Southwest Ledge with no wind pushing against the tide, the kind of stillness that usually means the water's about to tip over into something. Sure enough, when I ran the thermometer probe off the transom around the Ledge, I got a reading that told me what my gut already suspected: we're sitting right on the edge of a temperature break that could carry the first hardtails of the season. We flagged this a week ago — said a half-degree bump plus spring-tide mixing and late-July sun would push us into bonito water inside 7 to 10 days. Today's Day 7. I'm not going to tell you there's a bonito in the boat yet, but the water feels right, and I'd be scouting the Ledge and the rip off the north end with small metal — half-ounce Deadly Dicks, Albie Snax in olive — any time you've got calm glass and moving current.

The bigger story this week is what the bass are doing, and it's textbook August. Daytime, they've gone down and gotten quiet — sulking on structure in 40 to 60 feet around the Southwest Ledge and holding tight to the boulder fields off the North Rip, not up chasing anything you can see. I marked good bodies of fish on the meter around midday Wednesday sitting right on bottom, refusing to come up for anything, which is exactly what you'd expect with surface temps pushing into the mid-70s. The bite doesn't die, it just moves to the edges of the day. First light and last light, those same fish slide up onto the structure to feed, and that's when live eels fished on a fish-finder rig, or bunker chunks drifted back with the current, start putting bass in the boat — a mixed bag of schoolies with enough overslot fish mixed in to keep it interesting. Night has been the better play overall. Anchoring up-current of the Ledge and soaking eels after dark has produced some genuinely heavy fish this week, the kind that make you check your drag before you even make the cast.

Tides are the piece that's about to change things. We're sliding into a neap around August 5th and 6th, and I already noticed the current softening at the North Rip on Wednesday's ebb — nowhere near the strength it was running two weeks ago. We talked about this exact shift last week, that as the tides go soft the bass compress onto the strongest remaining current and the deepest, coolest structure, and that's precisely what I'm seeing set up. Over the next several days I'd expect the day bite to get even more stingy and the night bite at the Gut-style structure — deep water adjacent to hard current — to become the more reliable play. Lighter jigs, slower drifts, patience. Don't force a bass to bite in slack water at noon when you can wait three hours and get a real window at dusk.

Fluke are the one bright spot that hasn't needed any translation this week — this is peak season for them and the fish are cooperating. Drifting the sandy stretches and channel edges around the Southwest Ledge and out toward Block Island's south side, we've had good numbers of keepers, some pushing into doormat range, on white Gulp Swimming Mullets rigged on ¾-ounce bucktails, tipped with a strip of squid for insurance. The bite's been best on the back half of the outgoing, when the current's still got some push but isn't ripping so hard you can't hold bottom. Porgies have been thick around the same structure — anybody who wants a guaranteed bend in the rod with sandworms or clam on a high-low rig off the Ledge or around Point Judith's rock piles isn't going home empty-handed, even on the days the bass make you work.

Bluefish have been more of a rumor than a pattern out here so far. There's bait moving through — pods of bunker showing up in Rhode Island Sound waters — but I haven't seen the sustained blitzes here that they're getting to our west along the Jersey and Long Island beaches. That fishery lives and dies with where the bunker sit, and right now the biggest schools are holding closer to shore on the mainland side. If bunker push out toward the island in any real number, the blues will be on them within hours — that's just how it works — but for now it's scattered fish mixed in with the bass rather than its own dedicated bite.

Looking ahead, I'd fish the next few days around the low-light windows for bass, keep the eel bucket full for after dark at the North Rip and the Ledge, lean on fluke during the day because that bite's dependable, and keep one rod rigged light and ready for anything that looks like a hardtail cutting through bait on the surface. If the temperature break holds and the water stays clean, I wouldn't be surprised if the first confirmed bonito or albie report out of Block Island comes before next week's column.
